newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-DALGLISH SEEKS TO CREATE HISTORY AT NEWCASTLE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DALGLISH SEEKS TO CREATE HISTORY AT NEWCASTLE.

text.p: Having twice left managerial jobs at Liverpool and Blackburn because of the stress involved, Kenny Dalglish is clearly a glutton for punishment.

By succeeding Kevin Keegan as manager of Newcastle, Dalglish has taken what is currently the most demanding, difficult and, some would say, impossible job in English football -- making Newcastle league champions again.
It's a feat they have not achieved for 70 years.
Certainly, he does not need the money and it's not as if he needs the aggravation or the media spotlight that he will again be under.
Dalglish's love of the golf course is well-known, his awkward and tight-lipped relationship with the media equally well-documented.

But the real reason he has returned to a high-profile job that Keegan quit because of the stress involved is that he cannot resist the challenge of doing what no other manager has done before -- winning the English league title with three different clubs.
For Dalglish to achieve that in the soccer-mad city of Newcastle, still reeling from Keegan's shock departure last week, would arguably be the greatest testimony to the man's soccer skills.

To motivate a team that blew a 12-point lead in the title race last year, to take over halfway through the season and reach the pinnacle of the game that even the messianic Keegan failed to reach, would put the icing on the cake of a brilliant career.
Dalglish has succeeded Keegan before. He took his place in Liverpool's team in 1977 after Keegan left for Hamburg.

Keegan left Anfield as the undoubted "King of the Kop" but by the time Dalglish left the club in 1991 he had not only taken Keegan's old crown but also made it shine in a way Keegan could never quite manage.

Dalglish went on to play 515 games for Liverpool, scoring 173 goals, picking up five titles as a player and three as manager, one uniquely as player-manager when Liverpool completed the league and F.A. Cup double in 1986.

In 1978 he scored the winning goal in the European Cup final against Bruges, one of four in which he played. He was an inspirational figure whose sweet touch on the ball and clinical finishing ensured him a place among the game's greats.
At the same time he collected a record 102 Scottish caps and scored 30 goals for his country -- a record he shares with Denis Law.

But in the same way that Keegan stunned Newcastle with his departure last week so Dalglish shocked Liverpool when he quit midway through the 1990-91 season, when he also officially retired as a player.

In his recently published autobiography he described in detail the causes, which were mainly triggered by the Hillsborough tragedy in April 1989 when 96 Liverpool fans died on over-crowded terracing before an F.A. Cup semifinal against Nottingham Forest.
The aftermath of Hillsborough showed another side of the man who often comes across as dour and uncommunicative to the public.

But he earned an ever-lasting place in the hearts of Liverpudlians for the warmth and compassion he showed to the families of the victims of the disaster. He and his wife Marina attended many of the victim's funerals and helped them come to terms with their bereavement. Already revered by the red half of Merseyside, they loved him even more after that.

But two years later, the tragedy took its toll on him and Dalglish said at the time he quit Liverpool he needed a complete rest from the game. After spending the best part of eight months bringing down his golf handicap he returned as manager at then-lowly Blackburn, a club just beginning their long climb back to the heights they occupied a century ago.
With huge reserves of cash made available to him, he turned Blackburn into champions by 1995. That ended the club's 81-year wait for the title.
In comparison, Newcastle's wait is modest at only 70 years.
But Dalglish quit as Blackburn boss a month after securing the title, again saying he need a break from football.
He "moved upstairs" to become director of football, but it was an unhappy arrangement with him having increasingly little involvement.
He finally left Blackburn at the start of August and recently joined Glasgow Rangers, the club he supported as a boy, with a low key, part-time job as a youth development officer.
Dalglish made his first impact in soccer as a Scottish schoolboy international and at Celtic, Rangers' arch-rivals, where he scored 112 goals in 204 games in the first phase of his career.
He won Scottish championship medals in 1972, 1973 1974 and 1977 and Scottish Cup medals in 1972, 1974, 1975 and 1977.
He is the only player to score more than 100 goals in both Scottish and English League football.

Now Dalglish is bidding to make more history by taking Newcastle to the title. If any man can do it, he can, as long as he can keep his nerve if Newcastle are involved in a tight run-in to the title, while all around him a million Geordies are likely to be losing theirs.
